concepts.title: Quantum Computing
concepts.simple_explanation: A model of computation in which information is held in quantum systems (qubits) and processed by controlled quantum operations (gates), followed by measurement.
concepts.visual_explanation: Picture a standard computer processing electrical currents through silicon transistors, compared to a quantum processor steering the delicate physical states of microscopic particles.
concepts.technical_explanation: Quantum computers execute unitary transformations on statevectors in a complex Hilbert space, followed by projection onto computational basis states.
concepts.example: Simulating complex molecular interactions in chemistry that require an astronomical amount of classical memory.

concepts.title: Classical Bit
concepts.simple_explanation: A classical bit has a definite value of either 0 or 1 at all times.
concepts.visual_explanation: A classical bit can be pictured as a light switch that is either off (0) or on (1).
concepts.technical_explanation: Information is encoded into two distinguishable macroscopic voltage states representing binary elements {0, 1}.
concepts.example: A single transistor holding charge in a modern CPU or a bit in computer memory.

concepts.title: Qubit
concepts.simple_explanation: A qubit is the basic unit of quantum information described by a state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, with |α|² + |β|² = 1.
concepts.visual_explanation: Unlike a switch stuck on 0 or 1, picture a point on the surface of a three-dimensional sphere (the Bloch sphere) where the poles represent |0⟩ and |1⟩.
concepts.technical_explanation: A two-level quantum system represented as a unit vector in a 2D complex vector space (C²). Measurement in the computational basis collapses it to |0⟩ or |1⟩.
concepts.example: An electron spin (spin-up |0⟩ or spin-down |1⟩) or a superconducting artificial atom.

concepts.title: Superposition
concepts.simple_explanation: A quantum state can exist in a linear combination of basis states rather than being restricted to one definite classical value.
concepts.visual_explanation: Superposition is not a coin spinning or a hidden secret value; it is a wave-like physical state described by complex probability amplitudes.
concepts.technical_explanation: For basis states {|0⟩, |1⟩}, any linear combination |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ is a valid state if |α|² + |β|² = 1.
concepts.example: Applying a Hadamard gate (H) to |0⟩ yields (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2, giving an equal 50% chance of measuring 0 or 1.

concepts.title: Measurement
concepts.simple_explanation: Measurement in the computational basis yields 0 or 1 with probabilities determined by the squared magnitudes of the amplitudes, causing the state to collapse.
concepts.visual_explanation: When you measure a qubit, the delicate quantum superposition instantly resolves into a definite classical outcome (0 or 1).
concepts.technical_explanation: A projective measurement described by projection operators P0 = |0⟩⟨0| and P1 = |1⟩⟨1|. Outcome probability is P(m) = ⟨ψ|Pm|ψ⟩.
concepts.example: Measuring (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 yields either '0' with 50% probability or '1' with 50% probability.

concepts.title: Probability Amplitudes
concepts.simple_explanation: For |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, α and β are complex numbers whose squared magnitudes give measurement probabilities: P(0) = |α|² and P(1) = |β|².
concepts.visual_explanation: Amplitudes have both size and direction (phase), like waves that can peak, trough, or cancel each other out.
concepts.technical_explanation: Coefficients in the expansion |ψ⟩ = Σ c_i |i⟩, satisfying the normalization condition Σ |c_i|² = 1.

concepts.title: Interference
concepts.simple_explanation: Quantum amplitudes can add constructively (reinforcing each other) or destructively (canceling each other out).
concepts.visual_explanation: Like two ripples on water colliding: crest meets crest to make a higher wave, while crest meets trough to produce flat water.
concepts.technical_explanation: Because amplitudes are complex numbers, phase differences cause constructive interference (amplitudes add) or destructive interference (amplitudes cancel).
concepts.example: Applying H twice to |0⟩ returns deterministically to |0⟩ because the |1⟩ path cancels out and the |0⟩ path reinforces.

concepts.title: Entanglement
concepts.simple_explanation: Entanglement creates quantum correlations between multiple qubits such that their states cannot be described independently.
concepts.visual_explanation: Two qubits become linked like synchronized pairs of dice; measuring one immediately correlates with the measurement of the other, no matter the distance.
concepts.technical_explanation: A composite quantum state |Ψ⟩ in H_A ⊗ H_B that cannot be factored as a product state |ψ_A⟩ ⊗ |ψ_B⟩. Reduced density matrices have purity < 1. Does not allow faster-than-light communication.
concepts.example: The Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 gives either 00 or 11 with 50% probability each; outcomes 01 and 10 never occur.

concepts.title: Quantum Circuit
concepts.simple_explanation: A sequence of quantum operations (gates) applied to qubits over discrete time steps, followed by measurement.
concepts.visual_explanation: Like musical notation where each wire represents a qubit track over time, and musical notes are quantum gates transforming the state.
concepts.technical_explanation: A directed acyclic network of unitary gates acting on designated qubit registers, culminating in projective measurement.
concepts.example: A 2-qubit circuit with an H gate on wire 0 and a CNOT gate connecting wire 0 to wire 1.

concepts.title: Decoherence
concepts.simple_explanation: The loss of quantum coherence caused by unwanted physical interactions between the quantum processor and its surrounding environment.
concepts.visual_explanation: Like trying to keep a quiet whisper intact inside a noisy concert hall; environmental noise scrambles the delicate quantum phase.
concepts.technical_explanation: Non-unitary decay of off-diagonal elements in the quantum density matrix due to environmental coupling (thermal fluctuations, magnetic fields, stray radiation).
concepts.example: Thermal heat in a dilution refrigerator causing a superconducting qubit to randomly flip or lose its phase.

concepts.title: NISQ
concepts.simple_explanation: NISQ stands for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum, describing today's era of 50 to hundreds of noisy, imperfect qubits without full error correction.
concepts.visual_explanation: The early vacuum-tube era of computing, before reliable silicon microchips made error-free calculation trivial.
concepts.technical_explanation: Current era of quantum devices featuring 50-1000 qubits lacking fault-tolerant quantum error correction (FTQC), requiring noise mitigation.
concepts.example: Running hybrid algorithms like VQE on a 100-qubit processor where circuit depth is limited by noise.

concepts.title: Problem-Specific Speedup
concepts.simple_explanation: Quantum computers provide substantial advantages only for specific mathematical problems; they are not universally faster for all computing tasks.
concepts.visual_explanation: A graphics card (GPU) is vastly faster for 3D rendering than a CPU, but you would not use a GPU to run an entire operating system.
concepts.technical_explanation: Speedups depend on algorithmic structures (such as the quantum Fourier transform or amplitude amplification) exploiting quantum interference.
concepts.example: Simulating quantum chemistry or integer factorization with Shor's algorithm, versus ordinary tasks like browsing the web or word processing.

concepts.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Computing
concepts.simple_explanation: A practical workflow in which classical and quantum processors divide tasks, using classical computers for logic and quantum processors for hard quantum subroutines.
concepts.visual_explanation: A classical conductor leading an orchestra, calling in a specialized soloist (the quantum chip) for the most intricate solo passages.
concepts.technical_explanation: Variational architectures where a classical optimizer updates parameter angles for a parameterized quantum circuit in an iterative loop.
concepts.example: Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) or Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA).

concepts.title: Qubit Technologies
concepts.simple_explanation: Physical hardware approaches used to build qubits, including superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, and photonics.
concepts.visual_explanation: Like different automotive engine designs (gasoline, electric, rotary) that each attempt to achieve transportation using different physical mechanisms.
concepts.technical_explanation: Different physical realizations with trade-offs in gate fidelity, coherence time (T1, T2), connectivity, and scalability.
concepts.example: Transmon qubits cooled to millikelvin temperatures versus laser-trapped ytterbium ions in high vacuum.
